newsitem.title: INDIA: Higher prices, more exports can save Indian tea.
newsitem.headline: Higher prices, more exports can save Indian tea.

text.p: Only a sharp rise in domestic prices and a revival of exports can save India's tea industry, delegates attending a plantation conference said on Monday.
"Prices of tea must go up by at least 20 rupees per kg," said N.C. Kankani, a former president of the United Planters' Association of Southern India (UPASI).
At present tea prices are around 35-40 rupees ($1) per kg.
Kankani said that domestic prices could only rise when there was export demand, which at present had been very slack.
"Exporters need to be given an incentive of at least five rupees per kg to revive prices at domestic auctions," he said.
India's tea exports have fallen sharply since 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, which accounted for nearly half the total exports from the country.
The country's tea exports in 1995 totalled 163.70 million kg, up from the previous year's 150.70 million against 215 million in 1991.
Exports in calendar 1996 have been targeted at 180 million kg but Kankani said they would be around just 150 million.
Kankani said Russia preferred Sri Lanka, despite its prices being almost double those of Indian teas, mainly because of a long-term credit extended to Russian buyers.
He said India should also liberalise its credit policy for the tea industry so that it could match Sri Lanka, its long-term rival.
Indian Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah, who addressed the conference on Monday, said he would discuss the issue of credit to the tea industry with the finance ministry and the Reserve Bank of India.
Ramaiah said that the Indian tea industry should develop branded teas which could significantly improve its returns.
India's tea industry and trade have been making efforts to sell a special India blend in small, convenient packages to Russian and other CIS markets.
R.D. Vadera, UPASI vice-president said that it would be extremely difficult to compete against established brands as the promotional cost of introducing new brands was prohibitive.
"Nonetheless it should be possible to identify a few target markets on a selective basis and venture an entry. Sri Lanka has done it in CIS," Vadera said.
He said UPASI had set up a task force to devise a strategy to promote exports.
Vadera said India's domestic consumption of tea had not been more than 4.0 percent a year, which many felt was adequate.
